subtitle: The Transition from Elder to Ancestor
introduction: Among the Tswana people of Botswana, death is not an end but a transformation. When one dies, they 'graduate' from being an elder to being an ancestor. This profound belief shapes every aspect of Tswana funeral rites, elevating them from mere ceremonies of grief to sacred rituals of transition that connect the living with the spiritual realm. Because the Tswana believe in ancestral spirits (badimo), funerals are of paramount importance in their culture. The funeral is the primary forum in which people enact core values of caring and love for each other and build mutual connections. Funerals are elaborate affairs that can last a full week, involving the entire community in a complex web of rituals, obligations, and expressions of solidarity. The Tswana funeral is a rite of passage that offers resolution and closure, but it is also an intensely social event where identities and selfhood are shared across bodies and selves through sentiments and material acts. It is a time when the community comes together to honour the departed, support the bereaved, and reaffirm the bonds that hold society together.

beliefs.ancestor_role: intermediaries between the living and Modimo, watching over descendants, intervening in human affairs, requiring respect and offerings, and consulted through traditional healers and chiefs.
beliefs.fate_of_soul: Those who die with regrets or unresolved issues may become ghosts who haunt the living during the night. Proper funeral rites are essential to prevent a restless spirit that may bring misfortune.
beliefs.transition_to_ancestorhood: The funeral is the ritual bridge between life and ancestorhood. The deceased is ceremonially guided into the realm of the ancestors through a series of rituals that ensure peaceful transition and continued benevolent presence.

general_process.description: Due to strong family ties, death announcements are delicate and require excellent communication skills. Emphasis is given to informing closest family members first.
general_process.traditional_method: The uncle to the deceased travels from house to house to inform immediate relatives; a younger relative runs for greater distances. The messenger informs the 'head' of each household, who then informs the rest. A family elder informs the headman/chief of the ward, who calls a meeting to announce the bad news.
general_process.modern_method: Most communication is now through telephone and social media, but it is morally wrong to post about death on social media before core family members have been informed.
general_process.infant_deaths: If the deceased is less than six months old, announcement is only to close family members; mourning period is 24 hours, and only the elderly attend the funeral.

general_process.description: Extended family, friends, and neighbours gather at the deceased's home to offer condolences. This includes contributing physically or financially to enable a dignified funeral.
duties: Older women send young girls to collect soil to renovate houses in the yard.
Young able-bodied men bring logs of wood for cooking fire.
Others bring calabashes of sorghum and maize for mourners to eat during the week and on burial day.

general_process.description: The mourning period typically lasts a week, with prayers and gatherings daily at the deceased's home. Community members help with cooking and dishing food.
general_process.go_bula_lekesi: On the morning of the burial, the coffin is opened before sunrise for the final viewing of the deceased's body. This is done with great respect.

general_process.description: From the first day, members of the public, guided by a pastor or traditional healer, gather for prayers at sunrise and sunset. Purpose: to pray to God to welcome the deceased, console and comfort the grieving, and give moral support.

Burial traditionally takes place early in the morning, expected by seven o'clock everyone is at the graveyard. Sympathy is expressed by visiting the home; silence is maintained while the coffin is carried. Tea and possibly food are provided for visitors.
The immediate family may shave off their hair, wear black clothes for a specified period, and observe a period of seclusion and ritual purification.
A ceremony where the bereaved take off their mourning clothes and return to normal life, honouring the late and marking the transition back to ordinary life.

family_role_general: Ladies prep food and salads; men focus on meat. Activities are carefully assigned. Children mourning a parent are immediately assigned an uncle and aunt who become their new parents and assume parenthood roles. The person closest to the deceased sits on a mattress for the duration of the funeral; after the funeral, the family cuts off hair and wears black clothes as mourning.

cattle.cultural_significance: Cattle are deeply intertwined with identity and pride. An elder's herd symbolises years of hard work and perseverance; size of herd reflects status.
cattle.ritual_slaughter: Funerals often involve slaughtering cattle to feed guests. Some parts are shared with key family members (uncles and aunts) as a mark of love and bond with the departed. An elder said, 'To bury a man like that without slaughtering his own cattle is painful... an elder deserves a befitting funeral.'
cattle.motlhakanelwa_beast: The beast that is shared, symbolising sharing of resources, family unity, and honouring the deceased.
cattle.impact_of_disease_outbreak: During Foot and Mouth Disease outbreaks, movement and slaughter of cloven-hoofed animals are banned. Families improvised with chicken, samp and beans, cabbage, soup, and bogobe. Mourners felt the absence of beef as a loss of culture, honour, and identity.

hair_shaving.description: When a mother or close family member dies, children shave off their hair, usually performed by an uncle or brother of the deceased.
purposes: Serves as an invitation for others to come and support the bereaved.
Detaches and cleanses the mourner from the darkness attached to death.
Removes ties between the living and the dead.
Cleanses to thwart bad luck associated with death.
hair_shaving.belief: If hair shaving is not adhered to, it might lead to misfortunes and things going wrong.

mourning_practices.wearing_tattered_clothes: Wearing tattered clothes ('makatana') is a measure of relative poverty and humiliation during mourning. Particular clothes have multiple meanings and authorise participation of certain social groups.
mourning_practices.kapeso: A dressing ceremony where women in burial societies (diswaeti) ceremonially and ritualistically empower themselves through being garbed, enrobed, or dressed.

burial_societies.name: Diswaeti
burial_societies.description: Women-centred local institutions that organise and disburse emergency financial relief to members' households in distress due to death. Majority of members are women. Mortality occupies centre stage as an inspiration, not final defeat.
functions: Offer emotional and social support to the bereaved.
Regenerate kin relations rather than wear them out.

tribes.name: Bakwena
tribes.distinctive_features: Purification rites; tatodi (death reporting) following traditional pattern; central role of cattle.

tribes.name: Bangwato
tribes.distinctive_features: Week-long funerals; slaughtering cattle to feed guests; prayer sessions held daily; male elders bid farewell to departed sons in a customary practice.

tribes.name: Bangwaketse
tribes.distinctive_features: Tatodi (death reporting) practice that promotes botho (ubuntu) in socialisation, fostering sense of belonging, unity, and identity; ensures culturally appropriate death reporting respecting family hierarchies.

tribes.name: Batawana
tribes.distinctive_features: Adapted customs to Okavango Delta environment; cattle-rearing heritage and geographical isolation; community mourns and celebrates lives of leaders.

tribes.name: Bakgatla
tribes.distinctive_features: Memorial and condolence prayer services held daily; royal funerals follow elaborate protocols with royal cemetery; particular songs for funerals.

tribes.name: Balete
tribes.distinctive_features: Maintain own funeral traditions within broader Tswana framework, reflecting unique history and cultural identity.

tribes.name: Barolong
tribes.distinctive_features: Melaetsa (messages) have become important; singing of hymns and contemporary choruses pervades church participation; Mantsala ritual believed to keep bad luck away from mourning family, usually performed when death was unnatural. 'It is important to respect the culture in order to live longer.'

christian_influence.methodist_liturgy: Setswana burial liturgy is almost a replica of Wesley's burial liturgy, but no formal liturgical inculturation or contextualization. Methodist minister acts without prior arrangement.
christian_influence.blending_of_traditions: Many Batswana blend biblical teachings with pre-Christian beliefs, believing in diviners who communicate with ancestral spirits to benefit the living. Informal inculturation seen in graveside prayers just before interment.
christian_influence.ecumenical_funerals: Development of ecumenical funerals with interdenominational co-operation; tensions managed by local ministers while mourners try to console the bereaved.

ancestor_veneration.badimo: Ancestors are venerated and remembered through ritual observances. Once one dies, they become an ancestor.
ancestor_veneration.rituals: Traditional ceremonies and rituals held every year before the first rains to thank ancestors for good yields. Bojalwa (traditional beer) is brewed; a beast is killed, cooked, and taken to the hills where Badimo are hidden (place called Badimong or Difokeng).
ancestor_veneration.role_of_chief: Badimo can be appeased or venerated via the local chief (kgosi). Tribal rituals for blessing of boys' (bogwera) and girls' (bojale) initiation, and rain making (go fethla pula) also involve ancestors.

modern_changes.urbanisation: Burial societies have become more important as extended family networks are dispersed; mortuaries and funeral parlours have taken over some traditional roles; telephone and social media replaced traditional messengers.
modern_changes.impact_of_disease_outbreaks: Government restrictions can disrupt funeral traditions, e.g., Foot and Mouth Disease led to adapting alternative foods while still honouring the deceased.
modern_changes.enduring_importance: Community support remains central; slaughtering cattle still seen as ideal even if not possible; family roles and responsibilities are still observed; botho (ubuntu) remains the guiding principle.
modern_changes.spiritual_dimension: Belief in ancestral spirits remains strong; funerals are still seen as transition from elder to ancestor; those who die with regrets are still believed to become ghosts who haunt the living.

summary_table.distinctive_features: Purification rites; tatodi death reporting; central role of cattle
Week-long funerals; prayer sessions; male elder farewell rituals
Tatodi practice; promotes botho, unity and identity
Adapted to Delta environment; cattle-rearing heritage
Royal funeral protocols; memorial services; funeral songs
Distinct traditions within broader Tswana framework
Melaetsa (messages); Mantsala ritual for unnatural deaths
